annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygons are discrete building/block footprints for housing association ownership, not a reporting tessellation or full-area classification; the main phenomenon is selected property areas with attributes like corporation and percentages, so PatchDS.
Point features mark selected archaeological find locations/cesspits with addresses and photos, so this is a point object layer rather than measures or events.
Point features mark selected archaeological find locations; each point is a distinct site/object with location, caption, and object code, not a measurement or event.

These are selected archaeological site polygons, not a complete tessellation or reporting units. The layer represents bounded historical site patches with descriptive attributes, so PatchDS fits best; polygon topology also supports PlainVectorRegion.

The layer shows selected park/plantsoen areas where barbecue is allowed, restricted, or forbidden, not a full partition or reporting unit. That makes it a bounded phenomenon zone layer (PatchDS) with isolated polygons, so PlainVectorRegion is the best geometry.

Polygon boundaries mark selected protected conservation areas, not a complete partition or reporting unit. The layer represents bounded cultural-historical zones/areas of interest, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Point locations mark observation/inventory sites, and the main phenomenon is bee surveys/occurrences by year, so this is best treated as an event layer rather than objects or amounts.
Point layer showing locations of honey bee hives/colonies; the main mapped phenomenon is the numeric amount of hives/colonies at each location, so PointDS + AmountDS.

The layer is a zone-based soil quality map with polygons forming a near-complete tessellation; the categorical zone/soil-function classes indicate full-area thematic coverage rather than discrete objects or reporting units.
Point features represent individual trees with IDs, species, planting year, and management attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features represent individual trees (distinct, countable objects). Numeric fields like plant year and radius are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point features represent individual trees with species, planting year, height, and ownership attributes, so this is a discrete object layer rather than measurements or events.
Point layer of individual trees with species, tree number, owner, and planting year; these are discrete mapped objects, not measurements or events.
Point features mark discrete neighborhood compost initiatives at street locations; this is an object layer, not measurements or events. Numeric fields are attributes of the initiatives, so ObjectDS.

Polygons mark named camera areas tied to overlast zones, not a reporting-unit tessellation or full coverage. The low shared-boundary topology and isolated areas support PlainVectorRegion; the main entity is bounded phenomenon patches.
Point features represent individual trees (Canadian poplars) with IDs, species, district, and management actions. This is a discrete object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Points represent distinct sensor/camera installations of the Amsterdam crowd monitoring system; the decisive rule is object points, not amount or event.

Polygons are selected cultural-historical exploration areas, not a full administrative/statistical partition; this fits bounded phenomenon patches. Metadata indicates area-specific heritage zones rather than reporting units or full coverage, so PatchDS with PlainVectorRegion.
Point locations mark reported knotweed sightings/patches; this is a discrete object/presence layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Point features mark ecological bottlenecks/passages with status and realization year; the layer is about occurrences/interventions over time rather than static objects. Geometry is PointDS from the point features.

Polygons are isolated wind potential areas, not a tessellated coverage. The layer represents selected bounded zones for wind energy potential, so PatchDS is the best fit rather than AmountDS despite numeric capacity/output attributes.
Point features represent election stemlocaties with bubble sizes encoding vote counts/percentages; this is a point amount layer rather than point objects or events.

Point layer of reported oak processionary caterpillar nests/records. The map shows where nests are present or removed over time, so the decisive entity rule is Boolean presence/absence rather than amount or object counts.
Polygons are selected pedicab restriction/permission zones rather than a complete tessellation; the layer maps bounded regulatory areas/patches, not reporting units or full coverage.
Point features represent pedicab stands/pitches, i.e. distinct real-world facilities/locations. The decisive rule is point geometry with object meaning, not amount or event.
Point features represent individual addresses/Verblijfsobjecten with a derived non-residential function; this is an object layer, not a measurement or amount layer.

Polygons are discrete block-street areas, not a full tessellation of Amsterdam. The layer classifies each area into housing/amenities/work mix categories, so the main phenomenon is full-area thematic coverage.

Neighborhood/buurtcombinatie polygons form a near-complete administrative partition with high shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer represents reporting/statistical units (wijken/buurten) with codes and area attributes, so LatticeDS.

Neighborhood/combinatorial area units ('Wijken', 'Buurtcombinatie') form an administrative reporting-unit partition with strong shared boundaries, so this is a tessellation. The main phenomenon is statistical/administrative areas, not the numeric area field, so LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete administrative partition with strong tessellation topology; the layer represents reporting/statistical units (Buurten) with codes and area attributes.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete tessellation of Amsterdam area units; the layer is reporting/statistical units with codes and area, so LatticeDS.
City districts are administrative reporting units that partition the area, and the polygon topology strongly supports a tessellation.

City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition the city; the layer is a tessellation of stadsdelen, not a set of standalone objects. The decisive rule is reporting unit -> LatticeDS, supported by the district/borough context and shared-boundary polygon topology.

The layer is a complete administrative area partition of Amsterdam neighborhoods/districts/areas, so it fits VectorTessellation; the polygons are reporting/administrative units with codes and area values, which makes it LatticeDS.

The layer represents Amsterdam areas/neighbourhood-like reporting units that partition the city, with adjacent polygons and shared boundaries indicating tessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units -> LatticeDS.

The layer is a partition of Amsterdam practice areas/gebieden and seems intended as a near-complete set of adjacent regional units, supported by high shared-boundary topology. The feature names and district codes indicate reporting/administrative units, so LatticeDS fits best.

Polygons form a municipal practice-area partition with strong tessellation hints and names/codes of reporting areas; this is a lattice of administrative/statistical units rather than patches or objects.

Polygon layer of industrial noise contour zones; these are selected bounded affected areas, not a reporting-unit tessellation or full-area coverage. Entity follows the patch rule for bounded noise zones, with Soort values indicating contour bands.

Polygon classes form adjacent noise-band zones with high shared boundaries, so geometry fits tessellation. The layer is a contour/interval map of noise levels (dB classes like 55-60, 60-65), so the entity is ContourDS.
Polygon layer of noise-class zones with class bands like 50-55 dB and >70 dB; this is a contour/interval map rather than a reporting tessellation. The decisive rule is contour zone representation.

Polygon noise-contour zones with dB classes (50-55, 55-60, etc.); main phenomenon is contour banding, not reporting units or full-area coverage. Topology hint suggests plain regions despite many adjacent polygons.
Point features mark polling/stem locations (countable election venues), not measurements or events; numeric vote fields are attributes, so this is ObjectDS.
Point layer of discrete green roof locations/objects in Amsterdam; attributes like address, roof type, year, and surface area are object attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.

Land use polygons form a near-complete partition of the area (high shared boundaries, high fill, no overlap), so geometry is VectorTessellation. The layer is an area-wide land-use classification, so the entity is CoverageDS.
Point features represent identifiable historical buildings/structures and sites; the layer is a selection of archaeological objects with attributes, so ObjectDS is the decisive entity rule.

The layer represents three selectable Amsterdam boundary shapes (municipality/agglomeration/metropolitan region) used for area comparison, not a reporting tessellation. The polygons are discrete, with topology hinting isolated regions, so PlainVectorRegion. They are identifiable bounded geographic objects rather than coverage, lattice, or amount.

The layer shows selected dog off-leash, prohibition, and restriction zones rather than a complete administrative partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The polygons are bounded special zones/patches with seasonal restrictions, which fits PatchDS.

The layer maps selected green areas/parks and protected zones, not a full-area partition or reporting units. The polygons are discrete bounded areas, so PlainVectorRegion; semantically this is a bounded phenomenon zone/patch rather than object, coverage, or tessellation.
Point features represent individual private elm trees (distinct, countable objects). The numeric fields are attributes of each tree, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point locations represent distinct housing projects/facilities, each with a name, address, owner, status, and dwelling count; classify as object points, not an amount layer.
Point features represent individual chestnut trees, a countable real-world object layer with species and damage status attributes; the decisive rule is object points, not amount or event.
Point layer used to sample continuous climate/hydrology values (Maaiveld, GLG, GLG_maaiveld); this fits PointMeasuresDS rather than objects or amounts.

Polygon layer with strong tessellation evidence (high shared boundaries, many adjacencies) and the theme is flood risk bands by probability/depth, so this is a contour/interval-style regional classification.
Point layer of fixed market locations; each feature represents a distinct market object/place, not an amount or event. Time fields are attributes of the market objects.
Point features represent identifiable green monuments/bijzondere bomen sites with names, statuses, and registry links; this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point features represent individual monumental trees (distinct real-world objects); numeric fields are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point features represent discrete monuments/buildings/objects, not measurements or events; classify as ObjectDS under the points branch.

Point features mark actual current growth locations of protected wall flora; the main meaning is presence/occurrence at locations, not measurements. The counts are auxiliary annual attributes, so ExistenceDS fits best.

The layer shows NO2 measurements at monitoring locations, so the main phenomenon is point-based sampled measurements. The features are polygons, but they represent individual measurement areas/locations rather than a tessellating region coverage, so PlainVectorRegion fits best.
Point locations of NO2 monitoring sites; the main phenomenon is measured air-quality values sampled at points, so PointDS + PointMeasuresDS.

The layer maps selected gulch/affected zones around the Oergeul, not a reporting unit or full coverage classification. Polygon topology is sparse and isolated, supporting PlainVectorRegion; entity is a bounded phenomenon patch (patch/zone), not an object or lattice.
Point layer of sounding locations; each point samples measured subsurface values (e.g., Top_Pleistoceen), so the decisive rule is point measurements.

Polygon layer of named development neighbourhoods; they are bounded area zones, not reporting units or full-area coverage. Topology and naming suggest a tessellation-like set of neighbourhood polygons, but the main meaning is selected development areas, so PatchDS.
Point features for individual public toilet facilities and related toilet objects; the main phenomenon is identifiable objects, not amounts or events.

Polygons are neighborhood-like areas with high shared boundaries, so the geometry is a tessellation. The layer encodes overnight-policy zones with selection/condition rules rather than reporting units or full coverage, so PatchDS fits best.

Polygons form an area-wide zoning/standards partition with strong tessellation hints, and the categorical field indicates a full-area thematic classification (coverage) for parking standard categories.
The layer maps identifiable named parks and green spaces as discrete bounded objects; the polygons are isolated park footprints rather than a full tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion + ObjectDS.
Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units that form a near-complete partition, and topology strongly supports tessellation (high shared boundaries, many adjacent pairs, no overlap).
Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units and the polygons form a near-complete tessellation with high shared boundaries; classify as a lattice rather than an object or patch.

Region layer of postcode6 polygons used as reporting/administrative units tied to addresses. Despite many polygons, they are not a complete tessellation because overlaps and topology hints indicate discrete postcode areas rather than exhaustive coverage, so PlainVectorRegion + LatticeDS.
LineString infrastructure layer of streets/routes; metadata and attributes describe Amsterdam plus and main transport networks, so the decisive rule is network/route system.

The layer shows selected polygon zones for Amsterdam traffic priority networks rather than a complete tessellation; topology also supports PlainVectorRegion. The polygons are bounded network areas/priority zones, so PatchDS fits best.
Point layer of named locations/cameras/sensors; the decisive rule is object rather than amount or event, since each point marks a specific real-world site with a privacy statement.
Point features mark where privacy-related data processing activities/research occur; the layer is about occurrences of operations at locations, so PointDS with EventDS.
Point layer of distinct camera/sensor locations for the car fleet scan; each point is a named real-world object, not a measurement or event.

Point locations are stemlocaties/polling places, and the map’s main message is election results shown with bubble sizes proportional to vote counts and percentages. By the point amount rule, this is AmountDS rather than ObjectDS.

Polygon layer of localized rainproof drainage problem areas with binary drainage suitability (Mogelijk/Niet mogelijk). The polygons are selected zones rather than a full administrative tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS fits best.

Polygon regions are isolated hydro-unit areas rather than a tessellating reporting grid, so geometry is PlainVectorRegion. The layer shows selected Rainproof problem/solution zones for water-overload analysis, which fits bounded phenomenon patches rather than objects or coverage.

Polygons mark selected rainproof bottleneck/overlast zones rather than a full partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer represents bounded problem areas with urgency labels, fitting PatchDS rather than tessellation or object/reporting-unit classes.
Polygon zones mark localized rainproof trouble spots/affected areas from a simulation, not a reporting-unit tessellation or full coverage map; best fits bounded phenomenon patches.
Point layer of religious facilities/buildings with names and addresses; these are identifiable real-world objects, not measurements or events.
The layer maps sidewalk segments as line features, and the main phenomenon is sidewalk width/usable width classes and related quantitative segment values, so LineDS with AmountDS is the best fit.
Line geometries representing the snorfiets verkeersbesluit on roadway segments; this is a route/infrastructure network layer, not objects or amounts.
Point features represent individual public sports/playground facilities with names, locations, and attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point locations of city-farming sites; each feature is a distinct place/facility (object), not an amount or event.
Discrete named city-farming sites/terrain objects with names, addresses, and websites; polygons are isolated patches, not a tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion + ObjectDS.
Point features mark where space-seeking initiatives were established over time; the decisive rule is event-at-location rather than object or amount.

The layer is a line-based street system ('Major streets' / 'Stadsstraten'), so the decisive rule is network infrastructure on lines. The numeric line number is just an identifier, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Line geometry with transport network metadata; the layer represents district heating/cooling transport lines, so the decisive rule is network/infrastructure.

Polygons are buffered network segments for district heating/cooling lines, not a tessellating area layer; the decisive rule is network infrastructure, so ENTITY is NetworkDS and geometry is PlainVectorRegion.

Polygon layer of strategic housing plan areas/projects with max dwelling counts; these are selected development zones, not a full-area reporting tessellation or coverage. PatchDS fits bounded project/zone polygons, and the low shared-boundary topology supports PlainVectorRegion.
Point features mark named local food and urban agriculture initiatives with addresses and categories; this is a point object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Line geometries represent the tram/metro route system; metadata explicitly describes a transport network of lines and stops, so this is NetworkDS.
LineString features with tram/metro line identifiers and map description of stations, stops, and lines indicate a connected transport network rather than isolated line objects.

Point features represent tram stops and metro stations, and the layer is explicitly about the tram/metro network. Numeric radius is just an attribute, so the decisive rule is network with point locations.
Point geometry with named tram/metro stops; metadata says it visualizes the station/stop/line network, so the decisive entity rule is network infrastructure.

Point features mark distinct traffic-light-controlled intersections (named crossing objects). Numeric fields are attributes like IDs and dates, not the main phenomenon, so this is an ObjectDS point layer.
Line features represent road links in the traffic model, and the mapped values are traffic prognoses/volumes on those links, so this is a network-like line layer with amount as the main phenomenon.
Point features are election polling locations, but the layer mainly maps vote counts/turnout percentages and party totals per location, so this is a point-based amount layer.

Points represent individual trees (tree replacement layer). The decisive rule is object-at-point: each feature is a distinct real-world object with species, ID, planting year, and size classes, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features represent identifiable traffic information system objects (cameras, displays, polls, barriers) with names/IDs and attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Point features represent identifiable traffic information system installations (e.g., poles, barriers, cameras) with standplaats and type attributes, so this is a discrete object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Point features mark bird nesting locations / presence at addresses; the main phenomenon is occurrence of breeding birds, not amounts. Numeric year fields are secondary attributes, so classify as existence at points.
Point features represent individual park benches (distinct managed objects); the numeric/text fields are attributes, and the layer is about bench adoption status, not amounts or events.

Line features represent street segments/sidewalk stretches, and the layer maps walkability and pedestrian space/pressure classes along those segments. This is a line-based thematic amount/intensity map rather than objects or a network topology layer.
Point features represent discrete wall art objects at specific building addresses, so this is PointDS and ObjectDS rather than a measurement or event layer.
Polygons form a near-complete partition with strong shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer maps Amsterdam welstand levels as an area-wide thematic classification, so CoverageDS.

The polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam with high shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer maps area-wide welstand (architectural quality) classes across the city, which is a full-area thematic classification, so CoverageDS.
Point features mark WWII attack/incidence locations with dates; the main phenomenon is wartime occurrences over time, so PointDS + EventDS.

Polygon layer of housing plan project areas, not a full-area tessellation; features are selected development zones/patches with housing counts as attributes, so PatchDS. Geometry hint and isolated project polygons support PlainVectorRegion.
Point features mark discrete self-build plot/project locations, not measurements; classify as identifiable objects with point geometry.

The layer is a full-area thematic classification of building/roof parcels into suitability categories for solar panels, so CoverageDS fits. Although many polygons are adjacent, they are discrete roof/building regions rather than a true area partition, so PlainVectorRegion is the best geometry.
Point features represent detected solar panel systems; the main mapped phenomenon is numeric magnitude (panel count and installed capacity), so this is a point amount layer.
Points represent named swimming and play-water locations, i.e. discrete real-world objects/facilities, not measurements or events.
